title: Structure of Atom
tagline: Subatomic particles, atomic number and isotopes, historical atomic models, photons, orbitals, quantum numbers and electronic configuration.

sourceNote.boardprep: Original study material written by BoardPrep for the CISCE ISC Class XI Chemistry syllabus (official-verified baseline, examination year 2027). Syllabus unit and chapter title were taken from the official-verified ISC Chemistry registry entry; no board examination paper was consulted, so every question is original practice and not a previous year question.

overview.intro: An atom is the smallest unit of an element that still keeps that element’s chemical identity. For a long time, atoms were treated as indivisible, then experiments began to reveal particles inside them and a history of models that tried to explain what they looked like. This chapter follows that development: it starts with the electron, the proton and the neutron, looks at the important early models and what they could and could not explain, and ends with the modern picture in which we describe an electron not as a small planet on a fixed track but as occupying an orbital described by quantum numbers and filled according to a few simple rules.

learningOutcomes: Describe the discovery and main properties of the electron, proton and neutron.
Distinguish atomic number, mass number, isotopes and isobars.
Explain what Thomson’s, Rutherford’s and Bohr’s models could account for and where each model fell short.
Distinguish a Bohr orbit from an orbital and relate quantum numbers to an electron’s state.
Write the electronic configuration of simple atoms using the Aufbau principle, Pauli exclusion principle and Hund’s rule.

blocks.text: The three subatomic particles that matter most in chemistry are the electron, the proton and the neutron. The electron is negatively charged and has very little mass compared with the nucleus. The proton is positively charged and is found in the nucleus. The neutron has no charge and is also in the nucleus, and its mass is close to that of a proton. Together, protons and neutrons make up almost all of an atom’s mass, while electrons determine much of its chemical behaviour.

items: Electrons are negatively charged and are outside the nucleus.
Protons are positively charged and are in the nucleus.
Neutrons are neutral and are in the nucleus.
The number of protons in the nucleus is the atomic number.
The number of protons plus neutrons is the mass number.

items.text: A carbon atom with atomic number 6 has 6 protons. A carbon-12 atom also has 6 neutrons, so its mass number is 12; a carbon-14 atom has 8 neutrons, so its mass number is 14.
items.note: Same element, different mass numbers, because the number of neutrons is different.

blocks.text: The atomic number defines the element. If two atoms have the same atomic number, they are the same element. Isotopes are atoms of the same element with different mass numbers because they have different numbers of neutrons. Isobars are atoms of different elements that have the same mass number. These ideas are important because many properties depend on the number of electrons, which equals the number of protons in a neutral atom, not directly on the mass number.

items: Atomic number Z = number of protons.
Mass number A = number of protons + number of neutrons.
Isotopes: same Z, different A.
Isobars: same A, different Z.

items.text: Hydrogen has isotopes with mass numbers 1, 2 and 3, commonly written hydrogen-1, deuterium and tritium. Two atoms with the same mass number but different atomic numbers are isobars, because they are different elements.
items.note: The identity of an element follows the proton count, not the mass number.

blocks.text: Before we had the modern picture, scientists built models that each explained some observations but not others. Thomson’s model imagined the atom as a sphere of positive charge with electrons embedded in it. Rutherford’s gold-foil experiment led to the nuclear model, in which most of the mass and all of the positive charge are concentrated in a small nucleus, with electrons outside it. Bohr later proposed specific permitted orbits for electrons in hydrogen, which helped explain its spectrum but did not work well for more complex atoms.

items: Thomson: positive sphere with electrons in it.
Rutherford: small dense nucleus, electrons around it; explained some scattering results.
Bohr: electrons in permitted orbits in hydrogen; explained hydrogen’s spectrum but not much beyond it.
Each model was a step forward, not the final word.

items.text: If electrons were simply orbiting a nucleus like planets around the Sun with no further restriction, classical ideas would suggest they would lose energy and spiral inward; Bohr’s model tried to resolve this for hydrogen by restricting orbits.
items.note: Historical models are useful because they respond to real evidence, and also because their limits tell us why the modern picture is needed.

blocks.text: In the modern picture, an orbital is not a fixed path. It is a region associated with a high probability of finding an electron. Each electron in an atom is described by four quantum numbers: the principal quantum number, the azimuthal quantum number, the magnetic quantum number and the spin quantum number. The first two describe the shell and subshell, the third describes the specific orbital, and the fourth describes the electron’s spin direction.

items: An orbital is a region of high electron probability, not a fixed track.
s orbitals are spherical, p orbitals are shaped like two lobes.
The four quantum numbers together specify an electron’s state.
Pauli exclusion principle: no two electrons in the same atom can have all four quantum numbers identical.
Hund’s rule: in a subshell, electrons occupy separate orbitals singly before pairing.

items.text: The 1s orbital is spherical and closest to the nucleus. The 2p orbitals are at a higher energy than the 2s and are arranged in three mutually perpendicular directions.
items.note: Orbitals describe probability, so we talk about where an electron is likely to be found, not the exact path it follows.

blocks.text: Electrons fill orbitals in an order governed by energy and by a few rules. The Aufbau principle says that electrons occupy the lowest available energy orbitals first. The Pauli exclusion principle limits each orbital to two electrons with opposite spins. Hund’s rule says that when orbitals of the same energy are available, electrons occupy them singly before pairing. These rules together let us write the electronic configuration of an atom from its atomic number.

items: Aufbau principle: fill lowest-energy orbitals first.
Pauli exclusion principle: an orbital holds at most two electrons, with opposite spins.
Hund’s rule: occupy degenerate orbitals singly before pairing.
A neutral atom has the same number of electrons as its atomic number.

items.text: A neutral nitrogen atom has 7 electrons. Filling gives 1s^2 2s^2 2p^3. The three 2p electrons go into separate p orbitals with parallel spins before any pairing occurs.
items.note: Nitrogen is a good example of Hund’s rule because its p subshell is exactly half filled.

figures.description: A schematic moving from the nucleus outward to s and p orbitals, showing that orbitals are regions of probability, not fixed orbits.

keyPoints: An atom’s chemical identity is determined by the number of protons, the atomic number.
Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers; isobars have the same mass number but different atomic numbers.
Thomson, Rutherford and Bohr models each explained some evidence but had clear limitations.
An orbital is a region of high electron probability, not a fixed orbit around the nucleus.
Four quantum numbers describe an electron’s state; no two electrons in one atom can have all four identical.
Electronic configurations are built using Aufbau, Pauli and Hund rules.
examFocus: When asked for an electronic configuration, remember neutral atoms have Z electrons, and apply Hund’s rule within a subshell rather than pairing too early.
Do not confuse atomic number with mass number when identifying isotopes or isobars.

vocabulary.meaning: The number of protons in the nucleus of an atom.
The total number of protons and neutrons in an atom.
Atoms of the same element with different numbers of neutrons.
A region of space associated with a high probability of finding an electron.
A number that describes part of an electron’s state in an atom.
The arrangement of electrons in orbitals of an atom.

questions.prompt: The atomic number of an element tells you the number of:
questions.explanation: The atomic number is defined by the number of protons, not by neutrons or mass number.
questions.commonMistake: Thinking the atomic number refers to mass or to the neutron count.

questions.prompt: Two atoms of the same element with different mass numbers are called:
questions.explanation: Isotopes have the same atomic number but different mass numbers because of different neutron counts.
questions.commonMistake: Mixing up isotopes with isobars, which share a mass number, not a proton count.

questions.prompt: Write the electronic configuration of a neutral oxygen atom.
questions.explanation: Oxygen has atomic number 8, so a neutral atom has 8 electrons. Fill the lowest orbitals first and then place the remaining electrons in the 2p subshell.
questions.commonMistake: Writing the 2p electrons as paired too early instead of spreading them according to Hund’s rule.

questions.prompt: State one important limitation of the Rutherford nuclear model.
questions.answer: One limitation is that it did not explain why electrons do not spiral into the nucleus, or why atoms produce discrete line spectra.
questions.explanation: A good answer mentions that the model left the stability of the atom or atomic spectra unexplained.
questions.commonMistake: Saying the model failed because it had no nucleus, when the opposite is true.

questions.prompt: Write the electronic configuration of a neutral chlorine atom and explain how many unpaired electrons are in its 3p subshell.
questions.answer: Chlorine has atomic number 17, so the configuration is 1s^2 2s^2 2p^6 3s^2 3p^5. In the 3p subshell, three orbitals are filled singly first, then one pair is formed, leaving one unpaired electron.
questions.explanation: After the 3s subshell is full, the five 3p electrons occupy the three 3p orbitals singly before pairing, so one electron remains unpaired.
questions.commonMistake: Writing 3p^5 as a single group without discussing orbital filling, or forgetting that only one orbital is left with an unpaired electron.
